rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - two-year (2017-2018) replicated field experiment in a gray jujube orchard in Qiemo County, Xinjiang, with three micro-sprinkler amounts (2, 4, 6 mm/d) plus control, measuring microclimate, leaf gas exchange, yield and fruit quality. Q2: Section 3.3 and Table 4 - micro-sprinkler cooling significantly increased soluble sugar (by 2.7-6.5% in 2017, 2-4.3% in 2018) and yield of T2 and T3 in 2017; T2 highest yield each year, 6687 kg/hm2 in 2017 and 6748 in 2018; Section 4.2 yield increased 1.87-7.35% vs control. Q4: Sections 3.1-3.2, Tables 1-3, Figs 3-6 - authors measured the intermediate variables (air temperature, RH, computed VPD, leaf Pn, Gs, Tr) and regressed yield and soluble sugar against leaf Pn (Fig. 6), linking VPD reduction to Pn increase and to yield/sugar.
rows.notes: Technology field says 'drip' but the passage explicitly names micro-sprinkler irrigation, which is what the study tests (micro-sprinklers added over a drip-irrigated orchard); the study matches the passage, so no mismatch flagged. Q3: yield and quality measured by a single method (hand harvest and lab assays). Q5/Q6: one site, one crop, 500 m2 plots. Q7: authors say cooling 'can be appropriate' in arid/semi-arid regions and that effects are strongest with 4 mm/d at flowering-fruit set, but these are not stated as requirements from own findings. Q8: the only stated limitation concerns the 1-day leaf gas exchange record and that VPD may not explain all stress aspects; nothing stated about the yield/sugar result itself, so 'no' with doubt. Q9: Table 4 gives means of 3 replicates with letter groupings only; no SD/SE for yield or sugar (SE in Fig. 3 is for VPD and gas exchange, not yield).

rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 - two-year replicated field experiment with three micro-sprinkler amounts plus control in a jujube orchard, Ta and RH recorded half-hourly at four heights. Q2: Section 3.1, Tables 1-3 and Fig. 3 - micro-sprinkler application lowered mean air temperature by about 1.2-3.2 degrees C across heights and raised RH by about 11-17% relative to control; VPD computed from Ta and RH declined consistently with sprinkler amount (abstract: roughly 3 kPa to 2 kPa). Q4: Tables 1-3 and Eq. 2 - the pathway (lower Ta plus higher RH yields lower VPD) is measured directly for each treatment and phase (before/during/after spraying). Q9: Fig. 3 caption - VPD, Pn, Tr and Gs values are reported as mean +/- SE of three replicates.
rows.notes: Technology field says 'drip' but the passage names micro-sprinkler irrigation, which the study tests; no mismatch flagged. Q3: microclimate effect established by one method (Ta/RH sensors at several heights; VPD derived from the same sensors). Q5/Q6: single site, single crop, plot scale. Q7: effects were found to be larger in the lower canopy (0-100 cm), during/after spraying and with larger amounts, but these are gradients, not stated requirements. Q8: no limitation stated for the microclimate measurements themselves (the 1-day caveat concerns leaf gas exchange). Tables 1-3 give means with letter groupings only; dispersion for VPD comes from Fig. 3 SE.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract through references). Both claim rows cite the same sentence; the review classifies the technology as 'drip' although the passage and the study concern micro-sprinkler cooling applied on top of drip irrigation.
